summary: Every Hebrew noun is masculine or feminine — there is no neuter. The ending usually tells: nouns ending in stressed -ָה (דִּירָה, מִטָּה, מְנוֹרָה) or in -ת (דֶּלֶת, צַלַּחַת, סְטוּדֶנְטִית) are feminine; most others are masculine (בַּיִת, סֵפֶר, שֻׁלְחָן, טֶלֶפוֹן). A few must be learned: כּוֹס “glass” is feminine with no ending, לַיְלָה “night” is masculine despite its -ָה. People have their natural gender, usually in pairs: מוֹרֶה / מוֹרָה, חָבֵר / חֲבֵרָה, סְטוּדֶנְט / סְטוּדֶנְטִית. The article הַ does not show gender; you see it in the words that agree: זֶה / זֹאת, הוּא / הִיא, הָיָה / הָיְתָה.

examples

blocks.title: The plural does not tell the gender
blocks.text: חַלּוֹן → חַלּוֹנוֹת, קִיר → קִירוֹת, שֻׁלְחָן → שֻׁלְחָנוֹת, כִּסֵּא → כִּסְּאוֹת, מַפְתֵּחַ → מַפְתְּחוֹת are masculine although they end in -וֹת; נָשִׁים “women” is feminine although it ends in -ִים. Learn the gender from the singular.

blocks.title: Test it with זֶה / זֹאת
blocks.text: If you know the gender, you can say “this is a …”: זֶה בַּיִת, זֹאת דִּירָה, זֶה חַלּוֹן, זֹאת כּוֹס. The demonstrative, the pronoun (הוּא / הִיא) and later the adjective and the verb all show it.
You already met the exceptions in the greetings: לַיְלָה טוֹב (not טוֹבָה) shows that לַיְלָה is masculine, and בֹּקֶר טוֹב, עֶרֶב טוֹב are masculine too.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Is it a person? Then natural gender.
Does it end in stressed -ָה or in -ת? Then feminine.
Is it on the exception list (כּוֹס, לַיְלָה)?
Am I being fooled by the plural ending?

askYourself: Is it a person? → the person’s sex: מוֹרֶה (m.) / מוֹרָה (f.).
Does the singular end in stressed -ָה? → feminine (דִּירָה, מִטָּה).
Does it end in -ת (-ֶת, -ַת, -ִית, -וּת)? → feminine (דֶּלֶת, צַלַּחַת).
Otherwise → masculine (בַּיִת, סֵפֶר) — unless it is an exception (כּוֹס f., לַיְלָה m.).
Am I looking at the plural? → do not judge by -ִים / -וֹת; go back to the singular.

traps: Plural -וֹת does not mean feminine: הַחַלּוֹנוֹת הָאֵלֶּה are masculine (הֵם).
כּוֹס is feminine with no ending: הַכּוֹס הַזֹּאת, הִיא.
לַיְלָה is masculine despite -ָה: לַיְלָה טוֹב.
German gender is no guide: das Bett → מִטָּה (f.), das Buch → סֵפֶר (m.).
The article הַ is the same for both genders — it never shows the gender.

quiz.q: חַלּוֹן has the plural חַלּוֹנוֹת. Its gender?
quiz.why: The plural ending does not decide: הַחַלּוֹן הַזֶּה, הַחַלּוֹנוֹת הָהֵם — masculine.

quiz.q: Which noun is feminine although it has no feminine ending?
quiz.why: כּוֹס “glass, cup” is feminine in standard Hebrew: הַכּוֹס הַזֹּאת.

quiz.q: Which noun is masculine although it ends in -ָה?
quiz.why: That is why we say לַיְלָה טוֹב, not *טוֹבָה.

quiz.q: What shows the gender of a noun in הַסֵּפֶר?
options: nothing in the article — only the words that agree
quiz.answer: nothing in the article — only the words that agree
quiz.why: הַ is the same for both genders; זֶה / זֹאת, הוּא / הִיא and הָיָה / הָיְתָה show it.

quiz.q: German das Bett is neuter. Hebrew מִטָּה is …
quiz.why: Hebrew has no neuter; מִטָּה ends in -ָה → feminine.

seeAlso.note: Arabic has the same two genders; its feminine ending ـة (-a / -at) is the twin of Hebrew -ָה / -ַת, and Arabic too has unmarked feminines.
German has three genders and shows them in the article (der / die / das); Hebrew has two and shows them only through agreement.
Chinese nouns have no grammatical gender at all.
